content: Proponents of therapeutic ultrasound argue that it may alleviate pain by resolving inflammatory processes and reducing pressure on pain-sensitive structures caused by hematoma and edema. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of therapeutic ultrasound in managing acute perineal pain, persistent perineal pain, or dyspareunia, or a combination of these conditions, following childbirth. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched in January 2008 to identify relevant studies. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared active therapeutic ultrasound with no treatment, placebo ultrasound, or other standard or active treatments for women experiencing acute or persistent perineal pain or dyspareunia after childbirth. One reviewer assessed the quality of the trials and extracted the data. Four trials involving a total of 659 women were included in the review. The quality of the trials varied. In two placebo-controlled trials, women who received active ultrasound treatment for acute perineal pain were more likely to report pain improvement compared to those who received placebo treatment (odds ratio [OR] 0.37, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 0.69). However, no other outcomes in these trials reached statistical significance. In one trial comparing pulsed electromagnetic energy with ultrasound for acute perineal pain, women treated with ultrasound were more likely to experience bruising after treatment (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.60). Despite this, women in the ultrasound group were less likely to report perineal pain within the last 24 hours at 10 days postpartum (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.92) and less likely to report pain within the last week at three months postpartum (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.84). No other outcomes in this trial reached statistical significance. In a separate trial evaluating ultrasound for persistent perineal pain or dyspareunia, or both, women treated with ultrasound were less likely to report pain during sexual intercourse compared to those in the placebo group (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.84). However, none of the other measured outcomes in this trial reached statistical significance. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of therapeutic ultrasound in treating perineal pain or dyspareunia, or both, following childbirth.
